rapturous

RAP-chuh-ruhs · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Rapturous is full of intense joy or delight.

Reviewers were rapturous about the debut novel, calling it the finest first book in a decade.

Example

The crowd's rapturous cheers echoed through the stadium the moment the final whistle confirmed the underdog's victory.

This wasn't polite applause -- it was overwhelming, uncontainable joy, which is exactly the intensity rapturous is meant to capture.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ecstatic: Ecstatic names the feeling inside one person -- happiness so overwhelming that everything else disappears; an ecstatic winner may even stand frozen and speechless. Rapturous more often names what pours out: rapturous applause, rapturous reviews. Where ecstatic looks inward, rapturous spills over.

jubilant: Jubilant is the joy of triumph -- fists pumping after a win, a team parading its trophy. It needs something fought for and won. Rapturous is intense delight from any source at all: a favorite song, a perfect meal, an unexpected kindness.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

indifferent: having no particular interest or feeling

muted: restrained or subdued, without any strong feeling

Where it sits · how overwhelming the joy is — pleased → rapturous → transported

pleased vs. rapturous: Pleased is much weaker than rapturous: a pleased audience smiles and claps politely, while a rapturous one erupts in intense, overflowing joy.

transported vs. rapturous: Transported is stronger than rapturous: rapturous fans cheer with intense delight, but someone transported is carried even further, swept beyond ordinary self-control by emotion.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — rapture

root — rapture: a feeling of intense joy, as if swept away by it (from Latin rapere, 'to seize, carry off') (Latin rapere)

suffix — -ous

suffix — -ous: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Rapturous is simply rapture ('a feeling of intense joy, as if swept away by it') plus -ous, 'full of.' It comes from the same Latin root, rapere ('to seize'), as this unit's own rapacious -- one word seizes greedily, the other feels seized, swept away, by joy.

Use the root in a new word: rapture

Use the root in a new word: rapture: Watching the northern lights for the first time, she stood in complete rapture, unable to look away.

Root Check

Word Choice

Rapturous describes joy so intense it looks almost uncontrollable -- save it for reactions bigger than simple happiness. This unit's own rapacious shares that very same ancient root, rapere, 'to seize' -- rapacious seizes greedily, while rapturous feels itself seized, swept away, by joy.
